uncited: Voxels rasterized as geometry is an object-order volume rendering technique that treats volumetric data as a collection of 3D primitives (typically cubes or quads) and renders them using standard rasterization pipelines.
It solves the problem of visualizing scalar field data by converting it directly into mesh geometry, projecting it into screen space rather than sampling rays through the volume.
**Primitive Generation**: Each occupied voxel is represented by one or more geometric primitives.
**Coordinate Transformation**: Voxel indices $(i, j, k)$ are transformed into world space.
**Rasterization**: The generated primitives are transformed into clip space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix and rasterized.
**Culling**: To manage performance, frustum culling is applied to exclude voxels outside the camera view.
Each chunk is rendered as a collection of points using `GL_POINTS`, with vertex attributes for position, normal, and texture coordinates.
It binds the chunk VAO, sets model/view/projection matrices, and calls `glDrawArrays(GL_POINTS, 0, num_vertices)`.
A pitfall is that meshes are always updated on the GPU even if empty to prevent floating quads when destroying blocks near chunk borders.
The technique of rasterizing voxels as geometry has evolved alongside GPU capabilities.
Early implementations used OpenGL display lists for static volumes.
With the advent of vertex shaders and VBOs, explicit vertex buffers became standard.
More recent approaches leverage geometry shaders and instancing to handle larger datasets dynamically.
